projects.name: Technologies of Highly Interactive Computer Graphics

relationships.label: Milwaukee Coin and the Bally Brain
relationships.description: At Milwaukee Coin Industry, Dave Nutting asked Jeff Frederiksen to attempt an electronic pinball machine. Frederiksen designed a multiplexed switch-and-lamp system around Intel's 4004 and later 4040 processors. A side-by-side demonstration using two Bally Flicker machines convinced Bally management that the electronic controller worked and helped open the way for solid-state pinball.

relationships.label: The 8080 prototype and Gun Fight

participants.role: producer, pitch partner, and game contributor

relationships.description: Frederiksen replaced the dense TTL logic of contemporary video games with an Intel 8080 and a bitmap display. Nutting accompanied him to Midway with the unstable prototype and pitched Gun Fight to Hank Ross and Iggy Wolverton, who approved the project. A later historical account identifies Tom McHugh and Nutting with the game's software and describes Amazing Maze as a test program that became a commercial release.

relationships.label: Building the Bally Professional Arcade team
relationships.description: Nutting directed a multidisciplinary DNA staff that turned Frederiksen's custom-chip design into the Bally Professional Arcade and supported it with system software, cartridges, and a proposed computer expansion. Ogdon recalled joining a group of roughly twenty designers under Nutting, while McNeil identified Fenton, Lou Harp, and himself as core ROM programmers. The surviving accounts show a studio organized around specialist teams rather than a single author.

relationships.label: Astrocade software reviews
relationships.description: Tom Meeks recalled meeting Nutting and Ogdon's Chicago team almost every Friday while Astrocade still relied on DNA for software. Meeks brought test results and reactions from enthusiasts and public demonstrations; the developers used that feedback to revise games and remained open to outside suggestions.

relationships.label: Spectre Systems
relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey co-founded Spectre Systems with Michael Toth and Marion Nalepa. Bilbrey designed and programmed the games, Toth handled business arrangements and negotiated distribution through Esoterica, and Nalepa contributed sound to ICBM Attack.

relationships.label: Joining the DNA circle

participants.role: chipset designer, recruiter, and later employer

relationships.description: After Brett Bilbrey's reverse engineering exposed an intercept-register hardware problem, Jeff Frederiksen invited him to Chicago. Bilbrey remained at the University of Michigan and demonstrated his remote cartridge-development system by creating ICBM Attack and then Treasure Cove.

relationships.label: Brief overlap at Dave Nutting Associates
relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey recalled working briefly with Alan McNeil near the end of McNeil's time at Dave Nutting Associates. Bilbrey identified Dave Otto as the facility manager during the same period.

relationships.label: Action Graphics and Cosmic Raiders

participants.role: contract programmer assigned an early Defender-like version
Action Graphics head and released-game contributor

relationships.description: Dave Nutting and Jeff Frederiksen formed Action Graphics with Bob Ogdon, who served as president. The company contracted Brett Bilbrey after his two Spectre cartridges and supplied a DataMax UV-1 running TERSE. Bilbrey returned the system when the development method proved a poor fit; the released Cosmic Raiders was completed by Ogdon, Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting.

relationships.label: Technical publishing and user groups

participants.name: Fred Cornett
participants.role: Cursor editor and Peek & Poke Manual author

relationships.description: Brett Bilbrey shared reverse-engineering results, assembly routines, sprite techniques, and sound techniques through user groups and newsletters. He recalled teaching Fred Cornett material used in Cursor's Peek & Poke Manual and working with George Moses on several Bally Arcade projects.

relationships.label: From DNA to digital video
relationships.description: After DNA's game-development operation closed, Brett Bilbrey joined Jeff Frederiksen, David Shu, and former DNA colleague Dave Otto at Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories. Their digital-video frame-buffer work became Video Explorer and led to the Intelligent Resources–Integrated Systems spin-off.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade ROM and early software

participants.name: Jeff McKenna
participants.role: consultant who completed Bingo Math near ship time

relationships.description: Alan McNeil worked with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp on the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM. McNeil also credited consultant Jeff McKenna with completing Bingo Math near ship time, while his own work included DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, the ROM's interrupt and sound routines, Sea Wolf II, and the original TERSE engine.

relationships.label: DNA's Z80 development system
relationships.description: Alan McNeil recalled replacing DNA's crowded ModComp and Mostek-assembler workflow with a dedicated Z80 system. Terry Coleman and Tony Miller designed much of the probe, Jim Hemmer handled schematics, layout, and wire-wrap, Dave Nutting built the cabinet, and Dave Otto assisted with wire-wrap and day-to-day facility work.

relationships.label: Office mates and TERSE

participants.role: DNA cartridge programmer and TERSE user

relationships.description: Rick Spiece shared an office with Alan McNeil at Dave Nutting Associates. Spiece remembered McNeil creating the original TERSE engine and later used the language to prototype cartridge work before completing released games in Z80 assembly.

relationships.label: From DNA to Stern and Xtar
relationships.description: After leaving DNA, Tony Miller helped staff Universal Research Laboratories for Stern and recruited Alan McNeil first, followed by former DNA colleagues Terry Coleman, Jim Hemmer, and Bill Jahnke. Miller managed Berzerk while McNeil designed and programmed the game; McNeil later created Frenzy and briefly joined Miller at Xtar to work on a 3D project.

relationships.label: Bringing Tom DeFanti and ZGRASS to DNA

participants.role: UIC student, DNA engineer, and project connection

relationships.description: Leske studied under Tom DeFanti at UIC and introduced him to Dave Nutting Associates. That connection brought DeFanti's graphics-language work into the Bally computer-expansion project. After leaving DNA for Zilog, Leske later returned to work with DeFanti, although the surviving archive messages do not define his later responsibilities.

relationships.label: Programmable keyboard kit
relationships.description: With Bally's official expansion delayed, Leske worked with Bob Fabris on a programmable keyboard kit for Astrocade owners. When Fidelity Electronics appeared likely to acquire the system and revive the ZGRASS add-under, Leske chose not to compete with the expected official product and put his kit on hold.

relationships.label: Highly interactive graphics at SIGGRAPH 1984
relationships.description: At SIGGRAPH 1984, Leske presented “Software to Hardware: The Evolution of Highly Interactive Graphic Systems” as part of a course covering real-time entertainment, educational graphics, visual simulation, hardware, languages, and game design. The program identified him as a Chicago systems-graphics consultant and placed his session alongside contributions from Eugene Jarvis and other interactive-graphics specialists.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on

participants.role: hardware design engineer and productization lead

relationships.description: Larry Leske began DNA's Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on before leaving for Zilog. Tony Miller then took over its hardware, brought the prototype toward a manufacturable design, and helped connect it to a dual Micropolis floppy drive. Miller handled setup and support during public demonstrations while Jay Fenton presented the software, which included Alan McNeil's TERSE language.

relationships.label: Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC
relationships.description: Fenton created Bally BASIC as a compact programming environment for the Professional Arcade and later revised it as AstroBASIC. She also developed expanded and experimental variants, including Color BASIC, and used the language for programs such as Life and Nuke the @&#%$*. A December 1980 AstroBASIC assembly listing recovered from her original disks preserves the implementation.

relationships.label: Bally add-on and ZGRASS

participants.role: Bally hardware architect and add-on advocate
add-on hardware engineer and demonstration support

relationships.description: Nola Donato, Jay Fenton, and Tom DeFanti developed ZGRASS for the Bally computer add-on after DeFanti connected with Jeff Frederiksen at Dave Nutting Associates in 1977. Donato described herself as the principal author of the new Z80 language implementation; DeFanti credited the three programmers collectively. Frederiksen tied the language to the Bally hardware and promoted the add-on, while Tony Miller supported its hardware and demonstrations.

relationships.label: Robby Roto and Ms. Gorf
relationships.description: Fenton developed The Adventures of Robby Roto with Dave Nutting, then moved to Ms. Gorf after Robby Roto failed to find a large market. Contemporary 1982 footage records Fenton discussing Robby Roto and demonstrating the fast, still-silent Ms. Gorf prototype. The sequel was left unreleased when the arcade market contracted.

relationships.label: Preserving the DNA development archive
relationships.description: Fenton retained DNA disks, source listings, manuals, and an ICEbox development system for decades. Al Kossow began recovering the unusual disk formats, exposing Gorf, AstroBASIC, TERSE, and partial Ms. Gorf material. Fenton later donated the hardware and documents to the Computer History Museum, where the collection supports continued reconstruction of DNA's tools and software.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade hardware
relationships.description: Tony Miller worked at DNA while the Arcade's Address, Data, and I/O chips were being developed. He requested the BUZOFF signal so expansion hardware could isolate the custom-chip bus and return data to the Z80. Miller later described how Terry Coleman and Jeff Frederiksen verified the chip logic and how Jim Hemmer's printed-circuit work supported the console and later Stern team.

relationships.label: Early Bally Professional Arcade cartridges
relationships.description: Rick Spiece began at DNA in 1977 with Seawolf/Missile, developed on wire-wrapped emulator boards before the custom chipset returned from fabrication. He went on to create Panzer Attack/Red Baron and Grand Prix/Demolition Derby, then finished Mason's Blackjack/Poker/Acey-Deucey code and replaced its shuffle with Donald Knuth's algorithm.

relationships.label: Voltan video-pinball prototype
relationships.description: Spiece's most ambitious unreleased experiment was Voltan, a hybrid built from a conventional pinball machine with Astrocade-generated graphics placed behind the backglass. DNA constructed a single prototype, which Spiece believed was later dismantled for other work.

relationships.label: Bally Professional Arcade games
relationships.description: Bob Ogdon's first DNA assignment became Brickyard/Clowns, with Scot L. Norris contributing audio. Ogdon and Rick Spiece co-developed Football, and Ogdon later designed and programmed Bally Pin with Norris again handling its sound.

relationships.label: Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor
relationships.description: After his home-cartridge work, Bob Ogdon moved to DNA's coin-operated Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor teams. Ogdon credited Dave Nutting with the central ideas behind Gorf and Wizard of Wor. Fenton programmed Gorf in TERSE and worked within Ogdon's broader design group; the archive does not firmly establish that she programmed Wizard of Wor.

relationships.label: Coin-op designs brought home
relationships.description: Bob Ogdon adapted DNA's arcade work for the revived Astrocade as Space Fortress and The Incredible Wizard. As president of Action Graphics, he also supervised Dave Armstrong's first cartridge project, Quest for the Orb, using the studio's graphics-oriented development language.

relationships.label: Namesake of Berzerk's Evil Otto

participants.role: DNA facility and security manager and character namesake
former DNA engineer and Berzerk team manager who recorded the attribution

relationships.description: Tony Miller stated that the Berzerk team named Evil Otto after Dave Otto, the facility and security employee from their earlier workplace at Dave Nutting Associates. Alan McNeil's archive recollections independently document Otto's DNA role and the workplace friction surrounding it.

relationships.label: The Bally Arcade custom chipset
relationships.description: Jeff Frederiksen designed a custom chip set to replace much of the remaining TTL circuitry in DNA's processor-based arcade platform. AMI engineer Brian Taylor translated the design into 5-micron silicon. Frederiksen then shaped the same architecture into the Bally Professional Arcade, including a home-computer expansion connector. His later clock-driver letter and Bally-assigned bitmap patents document his continuing responsibility for the hardware.

relationships.label: From GRASS to GRASS3
relationships.description: At the University of Illinois Chicago, Nola Donato moved from molecular modeling into computer graphics and worked with Tom DeFanti on the PDP-11/Vector General GRASS environment. DeFanti credited his postgraduate student with generalizing the system's concepts into GRASS3; Donato later described the practical challenge of pairing artists with programmers around the early vector system.

relationships.label: Future-system research at Mattel Electronics
relationships.description: After moving to California, Nola Donato joined Mattel Electronics research. She evaluated and obtained advanced computers used to simulate proposed next-generation hardware, including comparisons between pixel-addressable and sprite-based display systems.

relationships.label: M2 system software
relationships.period: after the 1983 video-game contraction through the 1990s
relationships.description: After Mattel, Nola Donato worked on productivity software and hardware components with Intel and other companies. She later joined 3DO to write M2 platform software, briefly moving to game development after the M2 technology was sold before leaving when 3DO dropped the platform.

relationships.label: Keeping DNA's development operation running
relationships.description: Dave Otto handled facilities and security at Dave Nutting Associates while also helping with practical technical work. Alan McNeil remembered him doing wire wrap on the Z80 development system and handling phones and office duties; Brett Bilbrey recalled that Otto tightly controlled version releases. Those accounts place him inside the production workflow even though they do not identify him as a game programmer.

people.name: Alan McNeil
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates programmer, creator of TERSE, and contributor to the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM and early software.
people.astrocadeSummary: Alan McNeil worked at Dave Nutting Associates from March 1977 through April 1979. He helped build the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp, while consultant Jeff McKenna joined near ship time to finish Bingo Math. McNeil's credited console work also includes DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, and the system ROM's interrupt and sound routines. For coin-operated hardware he wrote Sea Wolf II largely in TERSE, the compact, FORTH-derived Z80 language he created for DNA. McNeil recalled that TERSE removed a layer of indirection from FORTH's inner loop and used 1 KB disk blocks rather than a conventional file system.
people.laterCareerSummary: Tony Miller recruited McNeil from DNA as Universal Research Laboratories staffed the Stern group that created Berzerk. McNeil designed and programmed Berzerk and later Frenzy; former DNA coworkers Terry Coleman and Jim Hemmer handled hardware and printed-circuit work. McNeil later joined Miller at Xtar for a time to work on a 3D game.
accomplishments: Created TERSE, the Z80 stack language used for Sea Wolf II and later DNA games.
Worked with Jay Fenton and Lou Harp on the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM and wrote its interrupt and sound routines.
Programmed DEMO, Speed Math, Gunfight, and much of Sea Wolf II; consultant Jeff McKenna completed Bingo Math near the console's ship date.
Helped replace DNA's shared ModComp-based workflow with a dedicated Z80 development system built around 8-inch disks and later CP/M experiments.
Designed and programmed Stern's Berzerk and Frenzy after leaving DNA.

people.name: Bob Ogdon
people.astrocadeRole: Game designer and programmer at Dave Nutting Associates, leader of a DNA development team, and president of Action Graphics.
people.astrocadeSummary: Bob Ogdon entered game development after his wife, Julie, introduced him to Dave Nutting. A psychology graduate of the University of Puget Sound, he moved to Chicago and joined the group developing software for the Bally Professional Arcade. His first assignment became Brickyard/Clowns, including the home translation of Exidy's Clowns. He went on to co-develop Football with Rick Spiece and to design and program Bally Pin. DNA then moved him into coin-operated work on Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor. Contemporary accounts describe those games as team efforts: Ogdon shaped designs and led developers rather than producing every part alone.
people.laterCareerSummary: When Bally withdrew from the home-console market, Ogdon became president of Action Graphics, formed with Dave Nutting and Jeff Frederiksen to continue Astrocade cartridge development. The company produced later work including Cosmic Raiders, credited in the archive to Ogdon, Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting. Ogdon also supervised Dave Armstrong's first project, Quest for the Orb, using DNA's graphics-oriented development language.
accomplishments: Programmed Brickyard/Clowns, with Scot Norris supplying the audio; Clowns was the system's first 4 KB cartridge.
Co-developed Football with Rick Spiece and introduced horizontal scrolling to create a larger playing field.
Designed and programmed the two-playfield Bally Pin, again working with Scot Norris on audio.
Contributed game design and team leadership to Extra Bases, Gorf, and Wizard of Wor under Dave Nutting.
Adapted DNA coin-operated designs for the home system as Space Fortress and The Incredible Wizard.
Served as president of Action Graphics and contributed to Cosmic Raiders with Scot L. Norris, Julie Malan, and Lisa Natting.
Supervised Dave Armstrong's development of Quest for the Orb.

sources.label: Electronic Games — Meet Bob Ogdon, archived in message #10791
Tom Meeks — Ogdon's DNA cartridge team (message #455)

people.name: Brett Bilbrey
people.astrocadeRole: Spectre Systems co-founder, Bally Arcade programmer and hardware designer, and later Action Graphics contract developer.
people.astrocadeSummary: While studying electrical engineering at the University of Michigan, Bilbrey bought a Bally Arcade, reverse-engineered its Z80-based hardware and ROM, and helped Spectre Systems build a TRS-80 development system that mapped expansion RAM into the console's cartridge space. His investigation of the intercept register and experiments with a light pen brought him into contact with Jeff Frederiksen, who invited him to Dave Nutting Associates. Bilbrey remained in school and used Spectre's tools to create ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove. He also designed and built the Spectre Systems controller used by ICBM Attack and intended for other games.
people.laterCareerSummary: After graduating, Bilbrey joined Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories after Bally's game-development operation at Dave Nutting Associates had closed. He later worked at Intelligent Resources–Integrated Systems and Intelligent Paradigm on computer and broadcast-video technology, including the Video Explorer frame buffer. He subsequently spent twelve years at Apple, where he led the Technology Advancement Group and worked on products and technologies including the Mac mini, Apple TV, and built-in iSight cameras.
accomplishments: Co-founded Spectre Systems with friends Michael Toth and Marion Nalepa; Toth handled business arrangements and Nalepa contributed sound to ICBM Attack.
Designed and programmed ICBM Attack and Treasure Cove using Spectre's custom Z80 development system.
Designed and built the Spectre Systems controller, combining an analog joystick, keypad, and side buttons for ICBM Attack and possible future games.
Published Bally Arcade assembly techniques and programs through The Arcadian and Cursor and shared discoveries with the Michigan Bally Users Group.
Preserved and shared source code, development notes, prototypes, tapes, and other early Bally Arcade material with the modern archive community.

Accepted an Action Graphics assignment for a Defender-like cartridge later released as Cosmic Raiders, but returned the UV-1 system after difficulty adapting to TERSE; he did not program the released game.

people.name: Dave Nutting
people.astrocadeRole: Founder of Dave Nutting Associates, early microprocessor-game producer, and studio leader behind the Bally Professional Arcade and many of its coin-operated and home-game teams.
people.astrocadeSummary: Dave Nutting owned Milwaukee Coin Industry, where Jeff Frederiksen developed the processor-controlled Bally Brain for an experimental electronic pinball machine. Nutting then backed Frederiksen's 8080 video-game prototype and joined him in presenting it to Midway; that work became Gun Fight and began DNA's long relationship with Bally Midway. At Dave Nutting Associates, Nutting assembled and directed the hardware, system-software, cartridge, and coin-operated teams that created the Bally Professional Arcade platform and many of its best-known programs. Coworkers describe him as both a studio leader and a practical contributor: he recruited designers, mentored Bob Ogdon, helped develop Gun Fight, originated important concepts for Gorf and Wizard of Wor, collaborated with Jay Fenton on Robby Roto, and even built cabinets for DNA's Z80 development systems.
people.laterCareerSummary: After Bally withdrew from the home-console business, Nutting and Frederiksen formed Action Graphics with Bob Ogdon to continue Astrocade cartridge development. Nutting later wrote Language of Nature: Quantum World Revealed and Secrets of the Creative Mind. Archive discussions sometimes confuse Dave Nutting Associates with Nutting Associates, the company associated with Computer Space; the latter belonged to his brother Bill and was a separate business.
accomplishments: Owned Milwaukee Coin Industry and authorized Jeff Frederiksen's attempt to replace electromechanical pinball controls with a microprocessor-based system that became known as the Bally Brain.
Took Frederiksen's barely working 8080 video prototype to Midway and helped win approval for Gun Fight, the landmark microprocessor-controlled arcade game.
Built Dave Nutting Associates into the organization that developed the Bally Professional Arcade hardware, system software, cartridges, computer expansion, and related coin-operated games.
Recruited and mentored a multidisciplinary staff that included Frederiksen, Jay Fenton, Alan McNeil, Bob Ogdon, Tony Miller, Tom McHugh, and other hardware and software specialists.
Was credited by Bob Ogdon with inspiring Gorf and Wizard of Wor, while DNA teams led by Ogdon and including Fenton turned those concepts into finished games.
Collaborated with Fenton on The Adventures of Robby Roto and continued to review Astrocade software with Ogdon's team after the console business changed hands.
Co-founded Action Graphics with Frederiksen and Ogdon to continue developing cartridges for the Astrocade platform.

people.name: Dave Otto
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates facility and security manager who also assisted with wire-wrap, release control, and practical support for DNA's development work.
people.astrocadeSummary: Dave Otto kept the Dave Nutting Associates operation running during the Bally Professional Arcade period. Alan McNeil remembered him handling security, phones, and some wire-wrap work on DNA's dedicated Z80 development system; Brett Bilbrey described him as the facility manager and recalled that Otto tightly controlled version releases. Ken Lill's description of surviving prototypes also attributes assembly of a gold Bally BASIC cartridge, dated May 14, 1981, to Otto, although that identification remains a collector's recollection rather than a production record.
people.laterCareerSummary: Brett Bilbrey later worked with Otto again at Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories and remained in contact with him. Jamie Fenton identified Otto as a possible lead to nine-track tapes that once held Bally Arcade, Gun Fight, Sea Wolf, and pinball source code. Otto also became part of video-game history as the namesake of Berzerk's Evil Otto: Tony Miller, who managed the Berzerk team after leaving DNA, stated directly that the team named the smiling pursuer after him.
accomplishments: Managed facility and security work at Dave Nutting Associates during the Bally Professional Arcade development period.
Assisted with wire-wrap and practical construction work on DNA's dedicated Z80 development system.
Controlled software-version releases at DNA, according to Brett Bilbrey.
Worked with Brett Bilbrey at both DNA and Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories.
Became the namesake of Berzerk's Evil Otto character, according to former DNA and Stern engineering manager Tony Miller.

people.name: Jay Fenton
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates system and game programmer who helped create the Bally Professional Arcade ROM, wrote Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC, contributed to ZGRASS, and developed Gorf, Robby Roto, and Ms. Gorf.
people.astrocadeSummary: Jamie Fenton, credited as Jay Fenton during her Bally and Dave Nutting Associates work, was one of the central programmers behind the Bally Professional Arcade. She worked with Alan McNeil and Lou Harp on the system ROM, wrote Bally BASIC and its later AstroBASIC revision, and created experimental versions including Color BASIC. Fenton also helped Tom DeFanti and Nola Donato develop ZGRASS and demonstrated software for the Bally computer add-on. In DNA's coin-operated work she programmed 280 Zzzap and Gorf, then developed The Adventures of Robby Roto and the unreleased Ms. Gorf. Surviving Gorf and AstroBASIC source recovered from her disks documents both her game work and DNA's TERSE-based development practice.
people.laterCareerSummary: Fenton later co-founded MacroMind and created VideoWorks, the animation program that evolved into MacroMind Director and then Macromedia Director. She subsequently worked in software and research, including at SRI International. Her preserved disks, documents, and ICEbox development hardware eventually entered the Computer History Museum collection, making original Bally, TERSE, Gorf, Ms. Gorf, and AstroBASIC material available for study.
accomplishments: Helped Alan McNeil and Lou Harp create the Bally Professional Arcade system ROM and its early software environment.
Wrote Bally BASIC and the later AstroBASIC revision; source dated December 1980 was recovered from her original disks.
Developed Extended BASIC and demonstrated the unreleased 32-color Color BASIC experiment.
Collaborated with Tom DeFanti and Nola Donato on ZGRASS and demonstrated software on the Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on.
Programmed 280 Zzzap and Gorf; recovered Gorf source confirms that the arcade game was developed in TERSE.
Developed The Adventures of Robby Roto and moved on to the unreleased Ms. Gorf after Robby Roto's disappointing commercial reception.
Created Astrocade programs including Life, Nuke the @&#%$*, and a 300-baud-to-2000-baud tape conversion utility.
Preserved and donated source disks, documentation, and an ICEbox development system used to reconstruct DNA's programming environment.

people.name: Jeff Frederiksen
people.astrocadeRole: Electronics engineer and chief hardware architect whose processor-based arcade work led from the Bally Brain and Gun Fight to the custom chipset at the heart of the Bally Professional Arcade.
people.astrocadeSummary: Jeff Frederiksen learned electronics in the U.S. Air Force and later joined Dave Nutting at Milwaukee Coin Industry. In a 2011 archive interview, Frederiksen described replacing an electromechanical Bally Flicker pinball machine with an Intel 4004/4040 controller housed in the “Bally Brain.” He then built an Intel 8080 bitmap-video prototype that Frederiksen and Nutting carried to Midway; it became the hardware basis for Gun Fight. Seeking to reduce the remaining TTL circuitry, Frederiksen designed the Bally Arcade custom chipset with AMI engineer Brian Taylor. Although conceived for coin-operated games, he deliberately shaped the Bally Professional Arcade for home use and included an expansion connector for a keyboard and computer peripherals.
people.laterCareerSummary: Frederiksen remained involved as the home system expanded toward a computer. At Astrovision's March 1981 sales meeting he demonstrated the revised BASIC interface, discussed the planned add-under, and presented ZGRASS with Tom DeFanti. His 1979 letter to Bob Fabris also documents a clock-driver repair for early Arcade hardware. After the video-game contraction, Frederiksen and David Shu formed Frederiksen and Shu Laboratories, where Brett Bilbrey worked on digital-video systems that led to Video Explorer. Frederiksen later worked in Apple's VLSI group.
accomplishments: Developed the Intel 4004/4040 Bally Brain controller and demonstrated solid-state pinball control to Bally management.
Built the 8080 bitmap-video prototype that became the platform for Gun Fight and DNA's later processor-based arcade games.
Designed the Bally Arcade custom chipset with AMI engineer Brian Taylor and adapted the architecture for the home market.
Held Bally-assigned patents 4,296,930 and 4,301,503 covering bitmap graphics techniques later licensed to Astrocade.
Supported the system after release through hardware fixes, public demonstrations, and the proposed ZGRASS computer add-on.

people.name: Larry Leske
people.astrocadeRole: Original hardware designer of the Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on and the UIC connection who introduced Tom DeFanti and ZGRASS to Dave Nutting Associates.
people.astrocadeSummary: Lawrence A. “Larry” Leske was a University of Illinois Chicago student of computer-graphics professor Tom DeFanti when he joined the Bally Professional Arcade work at Dave Nutting Associates. Tony Miller identified Leske as the engineer initially assigned to the computer add-on and credited him with connecting DeFanti to DNA. Leske left DNA for Zilog before the add-on was productized; Miller inherited the prototype and recalled that several of Leske's planned audio features were removed during the redesign. Leske later returned to work with DeFanti, tying the add-on's hardware lineage to the ZGRASS graphics-language effort.
people.laterCareerSummary: During the period when Bally's own expansion plans were uncertain, Leske also worked on a programmable keyboard kit for Astrocade owners. He put that independent project on hold when Fidelity Electronics appeared likely to revive the official ZGRASS expansion. By 1984, SIGGRAPH listed Lawrence A. Leske as a Chicago systems-graphics consultant. He presented “Software to Hardware: The Evolution of Highly Interactive Graphic Systems” in a SIGGRAPH course with Eugene Jarvis and other specialists in real-time graphics, education, simulation, and game design.
accomplishments: Began the hardware design for DNA's Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on before Tony Miller took over productization.
Introduced his UIC instructor Tom DeFanti to Dave Nutting Associates, establishing the connection that brought ZGRASS into the add-on project.
Planned audio capabilities for the original add-on design, some of which were removed during the later product-oriented redesign.
Developed a programmable keyboard kit for Astrocade users while Bally's expansion plans were stalled, then suspended it rather than compete with a possible Fidelity Electronics product.
Presented the evolution of highly interactive graphics systems at SIGGRAPH 1984 as a Chicago systems-graphics consultant.

people.name: Nola Donato
people.astrocadeRole: Computer-graphics programmer and principal ZGRASS language author who translated the GRASS approach to the Bally/Z80 platform.
people.astrocadeSummary: Nola Donato entered computing through molecular modeling and early vector graphics, then worked with Tom DeFanti on the original PDP-11/Vector General GRASS system at the University of Illinois Chicago. DeFanti recalled that Donato generalized GRASS's ideas into GRASS3 before the Bally project. After DeFanti connected with Jeff Frederiksen at Dave Nutting Associates in 1977, Donato, Jay Fenton, and DeFanti built ZGRASS for the proposed Bally computer add-on. Donato told Kevin Bunch that the different processor and display architecture required an essentially new implementation: she was the principal author of its language layer and made it more BASIC-like at Bally's request. DeFanti's own account credits the three programmers collectively, and surviving source listings preserve work by Donato, Fenton, and DeFanti.
people.laterCareerSummary: After moving from Chicago to California, Donato joined Mattel Electronics research, where she obtained and used advanced systems to model possible next-generation hardware, including comparisons between pixel-addressable and sprite-based designs. Following the video-game crash she moved into productivity software and hardware-component work with Intel and other companies. She later returned to game technology at 3DO, writing system software for the M2 platform before briefly moving to game software when the platform changed hands.
accomplishments: Helped develop the original GRASS computer-graphics environment and its GRASS3 successor at the University of Illinois Chicago.
Served as principal language author for the Z80-based ZGRASS implementation while collaborating with Jay Fenton and Tom DeFanti.
Co-authored “BASIC Zgrass: A Sophisticated Graphics Language for the Bally Home Library Computer” in 1978.
Left behind surviving ZGRASS assembly listings that document her implementation work.
Applied early graphics-system experience to hardware simulation at Mattel Electronics and M2 system software at 3DO.

people.name: Rick Spiece
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates cartridge programmer and prototype developer whose work ranged from the first Bally Professional Arcade cartridges to TERSE experiments and the Voltan video-pinball prototype.
people.astrocadeSummary: Rick Spiece joined Dave Nutting Associates in 1977. He identified Seawolf/Missile as his first cartridge and remembered developing it on large wire-wrapped emulator boards before the Astrocade chipset returned from fabrication. Spiece also developed Panzer Attack/Red Baron and Grand Prix/Demolition Derby, completed Mason's unfinished Blackjack/Poker/Acey-Deucey with a Knuth-based card shuffle, and co-authored Football with Bob Ogdon. He recalled using TERSE for prototypes while completing the released cartridges in Z80 assembly. His office mate Alan McNeil had created the original TERSE engine inside DNA.
accomplishments: Programmed Seawolf/Missile, beginning development on wire-wrapped hardware before the custom chipset was available.
Developed Panzer Attack/Red Baron and Grand Prix/Demolition Derby.
Finished Blackjack/Poker/Acey-Deucey after Mason's initial work and replaced its faulty shuffle with Donald Knuth's algorithm.
Co-authored Football with Bob Ogdon, combining Ogdon's football knowledge with Spiece's cartridge-programming experience.
Used Alan McNeil's TERSE language for prototype work before implementing released cartridges in Z80 assembly.
Created the Voltan prototype, which placed Astrocade graphics behind a traditional pinball backglass; only one experimental machine was built.

people.name: Tony Miller
people.astrocadeRole: Dave Nutting Associates hardware design engineer, Bally Professional Arcade add-on developer, and later manager of the Universal Research Laboratories team behind Stern's Berzerk.
people.astrocadeSummary: Tony Miller worked at Dave Nutting Associates while the Bally Professional Arcade and its three custom chips were being developed. His principal console project was the computer add-on planned to turn the Arcade into a fuller home computer. After Larry Leske left for Zilog, Miller took over the hardware, brought the prototype toward a product design, and helped interface it to a dual Micropolis floppy drive. Miller and Jay Fenton supported the machine at a late-1970s Winter CES and on a distributor tour through Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Seattle. The archive contains conflicting retrospective dates for those demonstrations and Miller's departure, so this profile keeps the chronology approximate.
people.laterCareerSummary: After leaving DNA for another coin-operated-game company, Miller helped staff Universal Research Laboratories for Stern. He recruited Alan McNeil first, followed by former DNA colleagues Terry Coleman, Jim Hemmer, and Bill Jahnke, and managed development of Berzerk. Miller later helped start Xtar, where McNeil briefly worked on a 3D game. In the Bally Alley archive, Miller also became an important technical witness, explaining the console's expansion bus, custom-chip implementation, video hardware, memory timing, and the add-on's history.
accomplishments: Took over the Bally Professional Arcade computer add-on after Larry Leske left DNA, completing working prototype hardware and moving the design toward production.
Supported the add-on with Jay Fenton at a Winter CES and during demonstrations for Bally distributors on the West Coast.
Requested the BUZOFF expansion-bus signal so external hardware could disconnect the custom-chip microcycle bus and return data to the Z80.
Helped design DNA's dedicated Z80 development-system probe with Terry Coleman.
Recruited former DNA engineers for Universal Research Laboratories and managed Stern's Berzerk development team.
Documented the Bally Professional Arcade's video and memory architecture for the preservation community and provided extensive firsthand technical corrections in the archive.
